phonemes.desc: Voiced alveolar stop [d], short [e], and aspirated voiceless bilabial stop [pʰ]; the phi is aspirated
Aspirated [pʰ] plus the diphthong [oi̯] — a rising glide from mid-back [o] to close [i]
The acute rides the final -οι diphthong, marking stress on the ultima of the plural place-name (Δελφοί)

pronunciation.approximation: 'del-PHOY-ee' — the middle syllable has a puffed 'p' and a diphthong like 'boy'; the final syllable is lightly stressed.

kin.label: Greek

kin.label: Latin
kin.form: Delphi, the Roman form that dropped the final diphthong glide

kin.label: Modern Greek
kin.form: Δελφοί (Delfoí), preserving the ancient name in contemporary speech

pronunciation.note: Delphoí is Tier 1: the acute on the final syllable marks stress, and the -οι diphthong it falls on is long, so the original Δελφοί carries both stress and vowel length. The aspirated [pʰ] is essential to the name; English 'Delphi' often loses the aspiration and the final diphthong quality.

domains.title: Oracle of Apollo
domains.subtitle: The domain of Delphoí
domains.lead: Delphoí is the sanctuary of Apóllōn on the southern slope of Mount Parnassos — 'the navel of the earth,' where the Pythia spoke the god's will from above the chasm. For a thousand years its oracle guided colonists, kings, and lawgivers; its games, treasuries, and hymns made it the shared bank and parliament of the Greek world.

mythology.lead: Delphoí sits on the southern slope of Mount Parnassos above the Gulf of Corinth, but in Greek myth it is the axis of the world. Its name was said to come from delphys, 'womb,' because the sanctuary marked the place where Earth gave birth to her greatest oracle. Before Apollo, the site belonged to Earth and the serpent Python; after Apollo, it became the voice through which kings, colonists, and philosophers heard the will of heaven. For centuries Delphi mediated between Greek cities and the divine. Tyrants and democrats alike sought Apollo's guidance; colonies were founded on oracles delivered from the Pythia's tripod. The sanctuary's prestige peaked in the sixth and fifth centuries BCE, when its influence extended from Sicily to the Black Sea, making Delphoi a panhellenic center of law, religion, and diplomacy.

myths.title: Apollo Slays Python
myths.text:
The Homeric Hymn to Apollo tells how the god, born on Delos, crossed the Aegean in search of a place to found his oracle. He came to Delphi, where a vast she-dragon named Python guarded the sacred spring. Apollo drew his bow and killed the monster, whose body fell into a cleft in the rocks; from that cleft rose the vapors that would inspire the Pythia, the priestess who spoke Apollo's words to mortals.

The god then established his temple above the chasm and took the epithet Pythios, 'Python-slayer.' Every eight years Delphi celebrated the Septeria, a ritual reenactment of the dragon-slaying in which a youth burned a hut representing Python's lair. The myth justified Apollo's ownership of the shrine and dramatized the triumph of Olympian order over chthonic power — and its ritual repetition ensured that the victory could never be forgotten as mere history.

myths.title: The Omphalos, Navel of the Earth
myths.text:
Zeus, wishing to find the center of the world, released two eagles from opposite ends of the earth. They met at Delphi, and the spot was marked by the omphalos, a rounded stone said to be the navel of the world. Pausanias saw the stone in the second century CE, covered with fillets and flanked by statues.

This centrality was not merely symbolic. Greek cities consulted Delphi before founding colonies, before declaring wars, and before enacting laws; the oracle was the closest thing the fragmented Greek world had to a shared court of appeal. The myth made geography into constitution: a people scattered across coasts and islands could act as one because they all faced the same center — the omphalos was the axle on which the whole scattered nation turned.

myths.title: Croesus, Oedipus, and Socrates
myths.text:
The most famous oracular consultations became cautionary tales about the ambiguity of divine speech. Croesus of Lydia asked whether he should attack Persia and was told that if he did, he would destroy a great empire. He attacked; the empire destroyed was his own. Oedipus, warned that he would kill his father and marry his mother, fled Corinth to avoid the prophecy and fulfilled it at Thebes. The Delphic god did not lie, but his words required interpretation that mortals often failed to provide.

Even Socrates received a Delphic response. The Pythia told Chaerephon that no one was wiser than Socrates, a pronouncement that set the philosopher on his lifelong quest to understand what the god could mean (Plato, Apology 21a). Delphi therefore stands not only at the center of the earth but at the center of Greek reflection on knowledge, hubris, and the limits of human understanding.

myths.title: The Pythian Games
myths.text:
Every four years Delphi hosted the Pythian Games in honor of Apollo's victory over Python. Founded, according to tradition, in the sixth century BCE, the festival included athletic contests, chariot races, and musical competitions in which players performed on the kithara and aulos. The earliest surviving notated music — the two Delphic Hymns to Apollo (c. 138 BCE) — was carved into the sanctuary's south wall, where it still teaches us the intervals of ancient Greek melody.

The games made Delphi a stage on which the Greek states performed their rivalry in a peaceable key: treasuries lined the Sacred Way as permanent advertisements of victory, and Pindar's Pythian odes turned the winners into figures of myth. The festival's real contest was between cities, and its real prize was prestige — the Pythian crown was proof that a polis could beat its neighbors with lyre and chariot as well as with fleets.

lore.syncretism: Under Rome, Delphoi kept its prestige without its power: emperors consulted the oracle and Greek cities still sent embassies, but the Pythia's answers grew rarer as the eastern oracles of Claros and Didyma rose. Christians read the sanctuary's decline providentially — according to late tradition, the emperor Julian's consultation of Delphoi in 362 CE drew the god's bleak reply that his spring had failed and his tripod stilled — and within two generations the oracle fell silent under Theodosius' closure of the temples. The site then passed through a Byzantine village to Frankish lordship; its stones went into the houses of Kastri until the French Archaeological School bought the village in 1891 and excavated beneath it. Rome, Christendom, and modernity each preserved Delphoi differently — as monument, as cautionary tale, and as dig.
lore.culturalLegacy: Delphoi never really ended. The excavations of the French School (from 1892) revealed the sanctuary that had slept under Kastri, and modern Delphi — a UNESCO World Heritage site — receives visitors on the same Sacred Way their ancestors walked. In European speech 'Delphic' became a permanent adjective for oracular ambiguity: every equivocal utterance of a central bank or a politician is 'Delphic' still. The two inscribed hymns to Apóllōn found on the sanctuary wall have been transcribed into modern notation and performed — arguably the oldest notated melody anyone has heard. And the maxim 'Know thyself' (gnōthi seauton), cut into the temple's pronaos, migrated from stone to Socratic philosophy to modern self-help without losing a syllable. Every four years a flame is still kindled at Delphi for international relays — a secular survival of the sacred fire that once burned above the chasm.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Delphoi is the ancient world arguing with itself about certainty. Every famous consultation — Croesus counting on a god who counted better, Oedipus outrunning a sentence that ran faster, Socrates made wise by a god who would not explain — ends at the same insight: the oracle never lies, but it never simplifies. 'Know thyself' over the door was not a greeting but a warning; the god's first demand was that the questioner know the limits of the question.

The restoration Delphoí belongs to that same honesty. English 'Delphi' has lost the aspirated phi, the final diphthong, and the accent that marked the word as a Greek plural — a name, perhaps, for the twin peaks above it. To write Delphoí is to keep the breath and the glide, the sound of a place where mortals once climbed to hear a sentence they would spend their lives interpreting.

lore.archaeology: The sanctuary's material record spans the Mycenaean age to late antiquity. A Mycenaean cult deposit with bronze figurines under the temple terrace attests worship from the Late Bronze Age. The fourth-century BCE temple of Apóllōn — the fourth on the site, funded by the Alcmaeonid family with a Parian marble façade — stands in reconstructed form on its excavated foundations. The Athenian treasury (c. 490 BCE), rebuilt in place, carried the inscriptions of the Delphic hymns; the omphalos (a Hellenistic marble copy in the Delphi museum), the Castalian spring, the theater seating five thousand, and the stadium where the Pythian footraces ran complete the complex. Excavations by the French School since 1892 also revealed the Marmaria sanctuary of Athena Pronaia with its celebrated fourth-century tholos.
